findings.headline: Council has committed £20m to Levelling Up Fund capital projects currently in progress.
findings.detail: Large capital enhancement projects are underway, described as delivering over £20m in public realm and historic environment improvements. These projects are intended to leave a legacy following the Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments carry delivery and financial risk. A lender assesses capital strategy, project delivery track record, and funding sources.
findings.figures: £20m total Levelling Up Fund projects
findings.quote: Several large projects are in progress, including the Levelling Up Fund projects, delivering over £20m of enhancements to the public realm and historic elements of Canterbury that will leave a legacy post-reorganisation.

findings.headline: Cyber incident is identified as one of the three highest-scoring risks on the Strategic Risk Register.
findings.detail: Cyber resilience is explicitly noted as a priority focus area. Cyber incident features alongside LGR and external relationships as top-tier risks, indicating material concern about digital security and potential operational/financial impact.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents can result in direct financial loss, service disruption, or compliance breaches. Identification as highest risk suggests material vulnerability exposure.
findings.figures: Risk score range: 20 down to 9; cyber listed among highest scoring risks
findings.quote: The highest risk scores were concerned with: • Local Government Reorganisation • Relationships with Trusts and other outside bodies • Cyber incident

findings.headline: Housing function underwent external governance review by the Housing Regulatory Inspector with formal action plan oversight.
findings.detail: The council has formally engaged with an external regulatory inspector on its housing function and is delivering a corrective action plan overseen by a dedicated Cabinet Committee. This indicates identified governance or service delivery issues in housing that require structured remediation.
findings.matters: Housing is typically a material financial function for councils. External governance review signals control weaknesses or service problems that could affect financial outcomes or compliance.
findings.figures: Not specified in this document
findings.quote: The housing function was recently reviewed by the Housing Regulatory Inspector. Delivery of the action plan arising from the review is being overseen by a Cabinet Committee.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 TM outturn report draft (2)_Oksana Ivanova MT
findings.headline: Council breached treasury investment limit on unsecured funds, reaching £7.18m against £5m policy ceiling
findings.detail: During 2025-26, unsecured building society investments reached £7.18m, exceeding the council's £5m policy limit. The council states the breach lasted 'one night only' due to timing of fund arrivals, and was corrected the next day. However, the council frames the £5m limit as guidance rather than binding policy, treating the exceedance as a minor administrative lapse rather than a control failure.
findings.matters: A treasury control allowing deviation from stated investment limits—even if brief—suggests the operational framework does not reliably enforce its own risk thresholds; this is relevant to assessing whether the council's treasury function can be relied upon
findings.figures: Maximum during year £7.18m; limit £5m; difference £2.18m
findings.quote: The balance went above this level for one night only, because funds arrived in the account after the cut off time for placing them into more secure investments fund. The £7m was moved out the very next day into higher security deposit funds, so the position was quickly adjusted.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 TM outturn report draft (2)_Oksana Ivanova MT
findings.headline: Whitefriars retail investment income remains below pre-pandemic levels, threatened by structural retail sector decline
findings.detail: Canterbury holds a strategic £79.2m investment in the Whitefriars Development Unit Trust. The investment generated £5.2m income in 2025-26, but this remains materially below pre-pandemic levels. The council attributes this to documented structural headwinds in retail: declining high street rents, online competition, and economic uncertainty affecting rent reviews. While low vacancy rates are maintained, income sustainability from this material asset concentration remains constrained.
findings.matters: A £79.2m retail asset in structural decline is a significant income risk; underperformance relative to historical norms suggests the valuation and future income projections may not be resilient to further sector deterioration
findings.figures: £79.2 million investment; £5.2 million income 2025-26; income below pre-pandemic levels
findings.quote: This strategic non-treasury investment generated £5.2 million of income in 2025-26. Income levels remain below those achieved prior to the pandemic, reflecting ongoing pressures within the retail sector. Nationally, high street retail rents have declined due to changing consumer behaviour, increased online competition, and continued economic uncertainty.

findings.headline: General Fund budget balanced through use of budgeted reserve drawdown of £0.4m with minimal surplus
findings.detail: The General Fund achieved only a £16,000 underspend for the year. The council had budgeted to draw £0.4m from its Budget Stabilisation reserve to balance the budget, and this occurred as planned. The Budget Stabilisation reserve ended the year at £3.4m after transfers to support other reserves and the General Fund Reserve.
findings.matters: Continued reliance on planned reserve drawdown to balance the in-year budget indicates structural revenue pressures and limited headroom to absorb unexpected costs or demand increases.
findings.figures: General Fund underspend £16,000; £0.4m reserve contribution used as budgeted; Budget Stabilisation reserve £3.4m
findings.quote: At the budget-setting stage, it was estimated the use of reserves to balance the budget for 2025/26 would be £0.4m from the budget stabilisation reserve.

findings.headline: Off-street parking income fell short by £404,000 at four city centre car parks due to Local Urban Fund works
findings.detail: Off-street parking revenue underperformed budget by £404,000, driven by closures or reduced capacity at four named car parks (Longport, Pound Lane, St Radigunds, Castle Row) affected by Local Urban Fund regeneration works. While other car parks performed to expectations, the concentration of impact on these four sites created a material shortfall.
findings.matters: Material dependency on parking income means that temporary disruptions from major works create revenue volatility; ongoing regeneration projects could create recurring income pressure.
findings.figures: £404,000 off-street parking overspend; four car parks affected by LUF works
findings.quote: Off street parking is reporting an overspend of £404,000, mainly due to income targets not being achieved at four car parks affected by LUF works: Longport, Pound Lane, St Radigunds and Castle Row.

findings.headline: HRA void property costs escalated by £1,617,000 driven by poor condition of properties on return and tenant damage
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance across the HRA overspent by £1,413,000, with void costs (preparing empty properties for reletting) alone overrunning by £1,617,000. The council attributes this to properties returning in poor condition requiring extensive clearance, garden works, and significant refurbishment, plus tenant-induced damage. Costs are under review but the council notes they will continue to require close monitoring.
findings.matters: Large, recurring void cost overruns suggest either capital maintenance backlog in the housing stock or underlying property condition issues, both of which indicate asset quality concerns and future expenditure pressures.
findings.figures: £1,617,000 void cost overspend; £1,413,000 total HRA repairs and maintenance overspend
findings.quote: Void costs continue to increase substantially with a £1,617,000 overspend. Costs are currently under review to understand the reasons behind this rise.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit overspend £831,000 due to subsidy rates not covering supported and temporary accommodation costs
findings.detail: Housing Benefit payments exceeded budget by £831,000 because the government subsidy (frozen at January 2021 Local Housing Allowance rates) does not cover actual costs for supported and temporary accommodation. The council explicitly states this is likely to continue as accommodation needs grow but subsidy rates do not.
findings.matters: A structural subsidy shortfall in a core service creates a recurring, unavoidable budget pressure that local savings cannot resolve and must be funded from the council's own resources.
findings.figures: £831,000 overspend; subsidy not covering full payments for supported accommodation and temporary accommodation
findings.quote: It is a challenge being faced by every council. Unfortunately, while the demand for supported and temporary accommodation increases, as do rents, we still only receive the subsidy amount based on the January 2021 LHA rates.

findings.headline: Interest and Financing Costs overspend £602,000 due to increased borrowing and higher interest rates
findings.detail: The council spent £602,000 more than budgeted on interest and financing costs driven by increased capital borrowing and elevated interest rates in 2025/26. This represents ongoing cost pressure as the council has expanded its debt portfolio into a higher rate environment.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs reduce financial flexibility and absorb money that could fund services. With rates remaining elevated, this is a structural pressure rather than temporary volatility.
findings.figures: £602,000 overspend; increased borrowing to finance capital expenditure; higher interest rates during 2025/26
findings.quote: Interest and Financing Costs are £602,000 overspent due to increased borrowing to finance capital expenditure and higher interest rates during 2025/26.

findings.headline: HRA energy efficiency investment stalled with £3.1m slippage pending assessment completion
findings.detail: Energy Savings Measures programme shows £3.087m slippage into 2026/27 due to delays in receiving retrofit assessments. The Retrofit Core Project Team is now assessing implications for the current and projected position through to 2028/29 to reprofiled budgets.
findings.matters: Significant delay to HRA energy efficiency investment affects the council's ability to improve housing stock condition and manage compliance obligations. Reprofiling through 2028/29 extends council exposure to this programme risk.
findings.figures: £3.087m slippage; programme extends through 2028/29; £1.5m grant repayment within this programme
findings.quote: The total budget slippage into 2026/27 for Energy Savings Measures is £3.087m

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme underspent by £7.5m with carry-forward slippage across all service areas
findings.detail: General Fund capital budget of £14.3m produced outturn of £6.3m, with £7.5m carry-forward requested. Slippage spans Corporate Services (£1.8m), People Services (£0.9m), Place Services (£2.4m), and Strategy & Improvement (£2.4m including £1.8m Levelling Up Fund match funding).
findings.matters: Large-scale slippage across all service areas suggests systemic delivery capacity or planning constraints, indicating the council may struggle to execute capital projects within forecast timescales.
findings.figures: £14.337m budget; £6.293m outturn; £7.523m carry forward; £521k net underspend
findings.quote: The total requested carry forward for the General Fund is £7.523m net (after taking account of specific grants, e.g. Housing schemes funded by housing capital receipts, grants and loans).

findings.headline: Warm Homes Social Housing Fund project delayed, requiring £1.5m grant repayment
findings.detail: The Warm Homes Social Housing Fund Project experienced significant delays in receiving retrofit assessments and progressing to design stage. No installation works were carried out in 2025/26, making a £1.5m grant repayment necessary. Negotiations with DESNZ to descope the first phase have been approved, creating opportunity to claim further 2026/27 funding, but the decision date is pending.
findings.matters: A £1.5m grant repayment materially affects cash flow and indicates delivery failure on a government-funded programme. Future funding of £6.6m depends on a pending DESNZ decision, creating uncertainty over the council's ability to complete the retrofit programme.
findings.figures: £1.5m of £1.9m 2025/26 grant must be repaid; original £6.6m allocation; further 2026/27 funding claim pending
findings.quote: There were significant delays in receiving the required retrofit assessments and subsequently progressing these to the design stage. As a result, no installation works were carried out in 2025/26. The consequence of this delay is that £1.5m of the £1.9m grant allocated for 2025/26 will have to be repaid.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve at minimum threshold with S151 officer emphasis on urgency
findings.detail: The General Fund Reserve is projected at £2m (1 April 2026) against a recommended minimum of £3m or 15% of net budget. The S151 officer explicitly advises that 'every effort must be made to achieve the agreed savings plan' and the council 'should avoid, at all costs' the reserve falling below 15%.
findings.matters: The reserve is at the minimum threshold with no buffer. The S151 officer's emphasis signals that any shortfall — from inflation, pay, or income risks already identified — will push the council below the safety level and force emergency action.
findings.figures: Estimated balance 1 April 2026: £2,000k; recommended minimum: £3m or 15% (net budget £25.84m = 15% = £3.88m)
findings.quote: The formal advice of the Section 151 officer to the council is every effort must be made to achieve the agreed savings plan in order to ensure financial sustainability and preserve the level of reserves for future commitments. The Council should avoid, at all costs, the General Fund Reserve balance reducing below 15% of its Net Service Expenditure.

findings.headline: Budget balanced in 2026/27 but requires £300k and then £1,150k savings in following two years
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget is balanced, but the three-year plan requires no savings 2026/27, then £300k in 2027/28 and £1,150k in 2028/29. The S151 officer states the council can no longer 'continue with that approach' of maintaining service levels and councillors must make 'very difficult decisions'.
findings.matters: The current balance depends on delaying savings; the council is signalling that service cuts are inevitable in the medium term, creating uncertainty about the sustainability of service delivery to justify borrowing.
findings.quote: The council has a successful track record in achieving a balanced budget while maintaining service levels, however in the current situation it will be impossible to continue with that approach. Councillors will need to face some very difficult decisions over the next few years in order to have a sustainable financial position.

findings.headline: Homelessness and rough sleeping funding reduced by £1.2m through grant consolidation
findings.detail: Direct funding for homelessness, rough sleeping, domestic abuse and discretionary housing payments falls from £2.8m to £1.6m. While RSG uplift is expected to offset this, the structural shift concentrates these services into a consolidated funding stream without ringfencing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether these services remain adequately funded under a new framework, and whether consolidation means funding shortfalls in one area will not be recoverable from the general fund.
findings.figures: Direct funding reduction from £2.8m to £1.6m
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the government has streamlined multiple service-specific grants into a single RSG. This consolidation includes previous allocations for homelessness, rough sleeping, domestic abuse and discretionary housing payments which now form part of the calculation for the council's CSP. As a result of this restructuring, direct funding for these services will reduce from £2.8 million to £1.6m.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will consume £500k annually from Budget Stabilisation Reserve
findings.detail: The council faces major structural reorganisation, with £500k allocated annually to LGR costs. This is described as requiring significant resource allocation, careful planning and robust governance. This drawdown reduces the reserve available to cover other risks.
findings.matters: LGR is a non-operational cost reducing available contingency. The timing and final costs are uncertain; £500k per year may prove insufficient if reorganisation requires more resource, further depleting reserves.
findings.figures: £500k allocated in 2025/26, further £500k each year
findings.quote: These changes will have significant strategic and operational implications for the council. In addition to maintaining core services and delivering business-as-usual activities, the council must allocate resources to prepare for LGR, manage the transition effectively and ensure continuity throughout the process. This will require careful planning, robust governance and a clear focus on prioritisation to balance transformation with ongoing service delivery.

findings.headline: Whitefriars property investment borrowing now depends on rental market volatility
findings.detail: Purchases in 2016 and 2018 significantly increased the council's debt, structured around rental income covering interest and principal. Income variability in the rental market creates direct repayment risk, requiring ongoing close monitoring.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council has taken on significant borrowing hedged against income that fluctuates with market conditions outside the council's control, reducing repayment certainty.
findings.figures: Purchases in 2016 and 2018; net income described as 'continues to stabilise and positively contribute'
findings.quote: The Whitefriars purchases in 2016 and 2018 increased the council's borrowing significantly. The purchase decisions were based on the rental income share covering interest and principal repayments, though with the understanding that the income will vary depending on movements in the rental market. The position will continue to be monitored closely as part of the budget management process.

findings.headline: Waste funding scheme introduces up-to-20% penalty risk based on future performance assessment
findings.detail: pEPR funding shifts to data-driven approach with modulation factors penalising underperformance. Council does not yet know the assessment criteria or how it will perform, explicitly flagged as a budget risk.
findings.matters: An uncertain income stream of unknown materiality has been included in the budget without visibility of how the council will be assessed, creating unquantified contingency risk.
findings.figures: Potential reduction of up to 20%
findings.quote: For 2026/27, funding payments will shift to a more data-driven approach and payments will be calculated using actual data submitted via the Local Authority Portal (LAP), incorporating both performance and recyclability metrics. Modulation factors, which penalise poorly performing authorities, will be introduced with potential payment reductions of up to 20% based on effectiveness assessments. The council will be notified on how this will be assessed and therefore this is a risk to the funding and budget assumptions.

findings.headline: Business rates reset triggers government top-up payment, exposing income volatility
findings.detail: The new business rates baseline of £5.46m is higher than retained income of £5.2m, requiring a £220k government top-up in 2026/27. This signals the council's business rates income will not naturally reach the baseline and depends on growth that may not materialise.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's income is dependent on government safety-net support rather than organic business rates growth, indicating structural weakness in the local economy or business rates recovery.
findings.figures: Baseline £5.46m; retained income £5.2m; top-up £220k
findings.quote: Retained business rates income for 2026/27 is projected at £31.4 million, offset by a tariff payment of £26.1 million, resulting in a net income of £5.2 million. This falls below the government's safety net threshold, triggering a top-up payment of £220,000.

findings.headline: Inflation expected to exceed budget allocation, with shortfall covered from reserves
findings.detail: The council has flagged inflation as a high-risk budget area, explicitly stating there is a high risk inflation will exceed available budget. Any overspend beyond contingencies must be funded from Budget Stabilisation Reserve.
findings.matters: This signals the budget is fragile: contingencies are already allocated, and management assumes additional inflation stress will erode reserves meant for other risks like LGR or income volatility.
findings.figures: Inflation contingencies allocated for Capital and Revenue; excess to be funded from reserves
findings.quote: Inflation is flagged as a budget risk and there is a high risk that it will exceed the budget available. In order to mitigate against this, additional inflation contingency budgets have continued for both Capital and Revenue. Any further inflationary increases not contained within the overall General Fund budget will need to be funded from the budget stabilisation reserve.

findings.headline: 2026/27 pay settlement unknown, budget built on uncertain assumptions
findings.detail: The national pay settlement for 2025/26 was 3.2%, but no information exists for 2026/27. The council has built its budget on assumptions, flagged explicitly as an area of considerable uncertainty that could require reserve drawdown if exceeded.
findings.matters: Labour costs are typically 40-50% of council expenditure; any settlement above assumptions erodes the balanced budget and forces further reserve use.
findings.quote: There is no information currently available about the pay settlement for 2026/27. Assumptions have been made in putting the budget together, but this is an area of considerable uncertainty.

findings.headline: Council subsidiary Canterbury Environment Company still £132k in debt three years after founding; not yet financially independent
findings.detail: Canterbury Environment Company, established February 2021, required a £220k cash flow loan to cover startup costs. As of end of 2024-25 (over three years later), the outstanding balance was £132k despite repayments having commenced in 2023-24, indicating the company has not yet achieved financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A council subsidiary unable to stand alone without cash flow support raises questions about the original business case and whether additional support will be needed, tying up council capital
findings.figures: £1m commitment; £220k drawn; £132k outstanding at end 2024-25; company established Feb 2021
findings.quote: The Council had committed to lending the subsidiary Canterbury Environment Company up to £1m for initial start up costs and cash flow. The company was set up in February 2021, a cash flow loan of £220,000 has been provided. Repayments commenced in 2023-24 and continue to be made; as at the end of 2024-25, the outstanding balance was £132,000.

findings.headline: Kent County Cricket Club loan carries £130k loss allowance (5.8% of £2.2m loan), indicating recognized credit risk
findings.detail: The council holds a £2.234m loan to Kent County Cricket Club. Accounting standards require a £130k loss allowance to reflect the likelihood of non-payment, leaving a net figure of £2.104m in the council's accounts.
findings.matters: A material loss allowance on a major service loan indicates credit concerns about a borrower; if the borrower fails, the council may not recover the full amount lent
findings.figures: Loan balance: £2.234m; loss allowance: £130k; net book value: £2.104m
findings.quote: Accounting standards require the Council to set aside loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment.

findings.headline: New PWLB borrowing restrictions eliminate property acquisition option; council ruled out future commercial property purchases
findings.detail: Government restrictions now prevent any council that purchases investment property from borrowing from the PWLB for any purpose. The council has explicitly ruled out future commercial property purchases citing this constraint as the primary reason.
findings.matters: The restriction locks the council out of a revenue-generation strategy and from PWLB borrowing access if policy changes; it represents a binding constraint on financial flexibility and borrowing options
findings.figures: None; this is a policy constraint affecting future capacity
findings.quote: If the Council decided to purchase any investment properties in the future, under new restrictions, this would prevent the Council from borrowing from the PWLB for any purpose. Therefore, for this, if for no other reason, it is recommended that the Council does not purchase any property for commercial gain.

findings.headline: Property valuations could fall below purchase cost; impairment would trigger revenue consequences and strategy reset
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that if the 2025/26 year-end audit values properties below their purchase cost (including transaction costs), this would constitute an impairment requiring both an updated investment strategy presented to full council and would have direct revenue consequences.
findings.matters: Property impairment would represent a loss to the council and could force a strategic reset of investment policy; it signals properties may not be holding their value in the current economic environment
findings.figures: Contingent on 2025/26 audit valuations; reserve/impairment thresholds not specified
findings.quote: Should the 2025/26 year end accounts preparation and audit process value these properties below their purchase cost, then an updated investment strategy will be presented to full Council detailing the impact of the loss on the security of investments and any revenue consequences arising therefrom.

findings.headline: Current economic climate significantly impacting rental income assumptions; forward-looking reserve adequacy at risk
findings.detail: The document explicitly flags that economic conditions are significantly impacting rental income assumptions for 2026/27, with reserves set aside to cover rental losses expected to be used this year. This suggests income pressure is expected to persist beyond the immediate Whitefriars issue.
findings.matters: If economic headwinds continue, further reserve drawdowns beyond 2026/27 may be needed, depleting buffers that protect the council against income volatility on its property portfolio
findings.figures: £2.917m reserve; part to be consumed in 2026/27; extent of ongoing pressure unquantified
findings.quote: The current economic climate is significantly impacting the Council's rental income assumptions for 2026/27 and reserves set aside to cover rental losses are expected to be used in this current year.

findings.headline: Whitefriars Development property generating insufficient income; £2.9m reserve expected to be drawn down this year to cover shortfalls
findings.detail: The council holds £75.6m invested in the Whitefriars Development Unit Trust. While rental income is described as stabilised, the document indicates that part of the £2.917m earmarked reserve will be required in the current year (2026/27) to cover income shortfalls. This represents an active drawdown of reserves specifically to manage income volatility on the council's largest single asset.
findings.matters: A major asset (£75.6m) whose income cannot cover its own costs raises questions about the investment's sustainability and whether reserves intended for broader council purposes can sustain continued income shortfalls
findings.figures: £75.6m investment; £2.917m reserve at March 2025; part of reserve expected to be used in 2026/27
findings.quote: It is anticipated that part of the reserve balance will be required in this current year to cover income shortfalls.

findings.headline: Whitefriars Development property is drawing on smoothing reserve to cover income shortfalls in 2026-27
findings.detail: Canterbury's £75.6m Whitefriars property investment was structured to set aside income above budget into a reserve to smooth income shortfalls during lease renewal periods. The council now expects to draw part of the £2.9m reserve accumulated by March 2025 during 2026-27 to cover income shortfalls, indicating the investment's income generation is not tracking as originally budgeted.
findings.matters: A major capital asset requiring reserve depletion to smooth income suggests cash flow volatility on the council's largest property investment; lenders need to understand whether income is temporarily suppressed or structurally weaker than expected.
findings.figures: £75.6m Whitefriars property value; £2.9m reserve balance at March 2025; anticipated partial draw-down in 2026-27
findings.quote: It is anticipated that part of the reserve balance will be required in this current year to cover income shortfalls.

findings.headline: Multiple prior-year improvement recommendations remain outstanding after 12 months
findings.detail: Of nine improvement recommendations from 2023/24, only two have been closed. Seven remain either in progress or have been superseded (requiring re-raising). This includes recommendations on Revenues and Benefits overspending, development of a comprehensive savings plan, workforce and asset strategies, HRA capital planning, and counter-fraud capacity.
findings.matters: Slow follow-up on audit recommendations signals weak implementation discipline and may indicate systemic capacity or prioritisation issues; it suggests prior weaknesses have not been remediated
findings.figures: 9 prior recommendations from 2023/24: 2 closed, 1 superseded (but reiterated), 6 in progress
findings.quote: It is recommended that the Council take immediate and comprehensive action to address the outstanding recommendations from the prior year, as outlined in appendix C. Failure to resolve these issues may undermine the Council's arrangements for ensuring value for money

findings.headline: Significant ongoing pressures from homelessness, income volatility, and funding uncertainty remain unresolved
findings.detail: The audit identifies that the Council faces 'significant pressures, including homelessness, income volatility, and funding uncertainty' that highlight the need for a formal savings plan with clear ownership. A prior-year improvement recommendation on Revenues and Benefits overspending (housing and temporary accommodation) remains in progress.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand pressures and income volatility can rapidly erode financial position; if homelessness and benefits costs are not managed, they will consume an increasing share of the revenue budget
findings.figures: No specific figures provided for pressures; prior recommendation on temporary accommodation and housing benefits overspending remains in progress
findings.quote: Significant pressures, including homelessness, income volatility, and funding uncertainty, highlight the need for a formal savings plan with clear ownership, governance, and monitoring.

findings.headline: Reliance on reserve drawdowns in place of structural savings, with £0.4m taken in 2024/25
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget is balanced only through use of the Budget Stabilisation Reserve. The Council drew £0.4m from this reserve in 2024/25. Auditors note this is a short-term solution that masks the need for lasting structural reform.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite; drawing them down year-on-year to balance budgets is not sustainable and signals inability to achieve structural balance through savings
findings.figures: £0.4m drawn from Budget Stabilisation Reserve in 2024/25; 2025/26 budget is balanced by use of reserves
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget is balanced and underpinned by prudent assumptions... the 2025/26 budget is balanced by the use of the budget stabilisation reserve

findings.headline: Draft accounts not published by the national deadline due to capacity constraints
findings.detail: Canterbury City Council missed the 30 June 2025 deadline for publishing draft financial statements. Accounts were finalised in late August 2025, creating a three-month delay. This is flagged by auditors as a capacity issue rather than a technical accounting problem.
findings.matters: Missed statutory deadlines signal resource constraints or governance weaknesses; they delay external assurance and limit stakeholder visibility into the council's financial position
findings.figures: 30 June 2025 deadline missed; draft accounts finalised late August 2025
findings.quote: The Council did not publish their draft accounts in line with the national deadline of 30 June 2025 due to capacity constraints. They were finalised in late August 2025

findings.headline: A £3.2m savings deficit over three years with no approved long-term savings programme in place
findings.detail: The MTFP projects deficits of £1.67m (2026/27) and £1.56m (2027/28), totalling £3.2m or 7.2% of net revenue expenditure over the planning period. The Council currently relies on annual service-level cuts and reserve drawdowns rather than a structured transformation programme with governance arrangements.
findings.matters: Without a credible savings plan and governance structure, the Council is exposed to forced service cuts or further reserve depletion; this directly impacts financial sustainability and ability to service borrowing
findings.figures: £3.2m total savings deficit over 2025-26 to 2027-28 (7.2% of net revenue expenditure); £1.67m in 2026/27 and £1.56m in 2027/28
findings.quote: The MTFP includes the detail of forecast deficits totalling £3.2m (7.2% of net revenue expenditure over the next 2 years after 2025/26)... we have as yet not heard plans for a longer-term savings programme being discussed nor discussion of the appropriate governance arrangements to support such a programme

findings.headline: General fund borrowing at £183m is significantly higher than peer district councils
findings.detail: The Council's General Fund borrowing stands at £183m, largely in long-term fixed-rate debt. The auditors note this is 'significantly higher than we see at other district councils.' The borrowing is based on the Council's overall requirements rather than individual projects or purchases.
findings.matters: High debt levels restrict financial flexibility and increase exposure to interest rate movements; lenders need to understand whether this reflects genuine capital investment or unsustainable spending levels
findings.figures: £183m General Fund borrowing
findings.quote: General fund borrowing levels are high at £183m and are largely long-term and fixed-rate... General Fund borrowing is significantly higher than we see at other district councils.

findings.headline: Pension fund data variance of £273k between council and pension fund records
findings.detail: A variance of £273k was identified between the benefits paid data submitted to the actuary by Kent pension fund for Canterbury City Council and the figure maintained by the pension fund. This has been recorded as an unadjusted error and relates to the £3.146m net defined benefit liability on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: Data integrity issues in pension fund records, even if unadjusted, indicate potential control weaknesses and create uncertainty around the accuracy of the £3.146m pension liability that affects the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £273k variance; £3.146m net defined benefit liability
findings.quote: We were informed by Kent pension fund auditors that they noted a variance of £273k between the benefits paid data submitted to the actuary by the Kent pension fund in respect of Canterbury City Council and the figure maintained by the pension fund. We have recorded this as an unadjusted error on page 49.

findings.headline: Land and buildings valuations understated by £2.1m due to valuation process errors
findings.detail: The auditors identified two errors in the valuations of the Royal Museum and Beaney Institute: the valuers used incorrect gross internal area (GIA) in the valuation, and an estimate for professional fees was omitted. These errors resulted in an £2.1m understatement of asset values, which has been corrected as an adjusted misstatement.
findings.matters: The £2.1m correction shows material errors in the council's asset valuation process, which forms the basis of £284m of land and buildings on the balance sheet. This represents a 0.7% error rate and indicates quality control issues in the valuation process.
findings.figures: £2.1 million understatement; £284m total land and buildings at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We identified two errors relating to the Royal Museum and the Beaney Institute, which resulted in an understatement of £2.1 million. These errors occurred because: The valuers used an incorrect gross internal area (GIA) in the valuation. An estimate for professional fees was omitted from the valuation.

findings.headline: HRA Reserve accounting error: prior years double-charged depreciation and borrowing costs
findings.detail: Management identified that in prior years, both depreciation on capital assets and the repayment of borrowing costs (MRP) were charged to the HRA reserve, creating a double charge. A prior-period adjustment of £5.984m was posted to correct this, increasing HRA Reserve and reducing the Capital Adjustment Account. Auditors challenged the appropriateness of applying a prior-period restatement and are awaiting management's response.
findings.matters: This reveals a systemic accounting weakness in how the council has been managing and charging costs to its Housing Revenue Account, a material reserve. The correction is substantial and indicates control gaps in reserve management oversight.
findings.figures: £5,984k prior-period adjustment to HRA Reserve
findings.quote: Management has posted a prior-period adjustment, which has increased the HRA Reserve by £5,984k and reduced the Capital Adjustment Account by the same amount. We have reviewed the approved MRP policies and noted that the changes to the MRP charging methodology were formally approved in the 2024/25 MRP policy. As a result, we challenged management over the appropriateness of applying a prior-period restatement. We are awaiting management's response to conclude on this matter.

findings.headline: HRA accounting treatment change increases reported reserves by £5.5m via principal repayment reclassification
findings.detail: The council has changed the accounting treatment of HRA loan principal repayment, deciding to stop charging it to revenue and instead treat it differently. This creates a £5.5m favorable variance. The paper notes this is 'a form of voluntary Minimum Revenue Provision' that was previously reducing the capital financing requirement.
findings.matters: This is a one-off accounting adjustment, not improved operating performance. It may signal that the HRA is under financial pressure and the council is using accounting flexibility to manage reported reserves. The change also affects how transparent the HRA's true revenue cost is.
findings.figures: £5,572,000 forecast underspend in Self-Financing Debt line
findings.quote: The loan repayment has previously been charged to revenue which means it is a form of voluntary Minimum Revenue Provision which reduces the capital financing requirement. This is not required in the HRA as it is covered by the depreciation charged to revenue. As per the explanation above, the decision has been taken to stop charging the loan principal repayment to revenue to replenish the HRA working balance.

findings.headline: Administrative Offices holding £172,000 recurring overspend from dual-site occupancy and security costs
findings.detail: Administrative Offices are £172,000 over budget due to ongoing business rates payments for the Military Road site, unbudgeted security costs at both Military Road and Rose Lane, and £43,000 in furniture removal costs for moving between temporary accommodation and a storage centre. This suggests the council is paying for multiple properties during a transition.
findings.matters: The overlap in occupancy and security costs suggests inefficient space management. The mention of temporary accommodation suggests longer-term estate restructuring may be underway, with costs accumulating during the transition.
findings.figures: £172,000 overspend including £43,000 furniture removal and ongoing business rates for Military Road site
findings.quote: The main overspends are due to ongoing business rates payments for the Military Road site and additional unbudgeted security costs incurred for both the Military Road and Rose Lane sites. In addition, there is a £43,000 forecasted overspend on removal expenses that are in relation to the moving of furniture between the temporary accommodation and storage centre.

findings.headline: Off-street parking revenue shortfall including unusual backdated electricity charges
findings.detail: Off-street parking is forecasting a £190,000 overspend. While part of this is due to car park closures during LUF improvement works (partly recoverable), a major contributor is electricity costs at Riverside Car Park including backdated charges spanning 2.5 years. This suggests a facility management issue.
findings.matters: The £190,000 overspend shows both short-term disruption from capital works and an underlying facility cost problem. Backdated charges over 2.5 years suggests a billing or accounting issue that may affect other services.
findings.figures: £190,000 forecast overspend; recovered ~50% of Castle Row Car Park closure income
findings.quote: The off-street parking service is forecasting an overspend of £190,000. A significant portion of the overspend is due to underperformance in car parks that were partially closed throughout the first part of the year for the LUF works... Another major contributor to the overspend is the electricity costs at Riverside Car Park including backdated charges for 2.5 years.

findings.headline: HRA tenant arrears and bad debt provision rising unexpectedly
findings.detail: The bad debt provision for the HRA has increased by £50,000 due to higher tenant arrears than originally estimated. The council is now using actual rent week 25 arrears data and has adjusted bad debt forecasts upward accordingly.
findings.matters: Rising arrears suggest tenant financial stress or payment behaviour change. An increase in bad debt provision at Q2 indicates the issue is material enough to adjust the year-end forecast, not noise.
findings.figures: £50,000 additional bad debt provision forecast
findings.quote: The original budget was set based on estimated arrears levels, the age profile of those arrears, and anticipated in-year write-offs. The current forecast reflects the actual arrears position at rent week 25, with assumptions applied for the age of arrears and expected write-offs for the remainder of the year. The increase is primarily due to higher arrears levels than originally estimated, which has resulted in a greater forecast provision requirement.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law creating new disrepair liability of £77,000 in HRA
findings.detail: Following implementation of Awaab's Law (the regulations requiring timely repair of hazardous defects in rental housing), the council is forecasting a £77,000 overspend due to anticipated increase in disrepair claims. This is a new cost driver created by the regulatory change.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law represents a new statutory obligation with financial consequences that are only now being estimated. The £77,000 forecast may be conservative if claims exceed expectations or if remediation costs rise.
findings.figures: £77,000 forecast overspend
findings.quote: Following the implementation of Awaab's Law, an increase in disrepair claims is anticipated, resulting in a forecast overspend of £77,000 against the current budget.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy falling short against rising demand for supported and temporary accommodation
findings.detail: Revenues and Benefits is forecasting a £541,000 overspend driven by Housing Benefit payments exceeding subsidy. The subsidy is frozen at January 2021 LHA rates while rents and demand for supported and temporary accommodation have risen. The paper flags this as a national problem with no mitigation strategy yet identified.
findings.matters: This is a structural revenue pressure created by central government policy, not a council control issue. It will likely persist and worsen as rents continue to rise, and the paper explicitly states 'ways to mitigate the shortfalls are actively being sought' — implying no solution is currently in place.
findings.figures: £541,000 forecast overspend; subsidy frozen at January 2021 rates
findings.quote: This is mainly due to higher-than-estimated Housing Benefit payments and the subsidy grant not covering all Housing Benefit payments in full. This overspend is consistent with national problems in this area with subsidies falling short in three main areas: supported accommodation, temporary accommodation, identified overpayments. It is a challenge being faced by every council. Unfortunately, while the demand for supported and temporary accommodation increases, as do rents, we still only receive the subsidy amount based on the January 2021 LHA rates.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account repairs and maintenance £1.95m over budget with unclear cost drivers
findings.detail: The HRA repairs budget has overrun by £1.95m in the first half of the year. The repairs-to-buildings price-per-property contract is £523,000 overspent and non-PPP repairs are £965,000 overspent, with investigations ongoing into contract scope and accuracy. Void costs are running £508,000 over budget, driven by higher property clearance costs and, according to early analysis, tenant damage and poor property condition at handback.
findings.matters: A £1.95m variance on repairs alone at Q2 suggests either serious facility deterioration, contractor cost drift, or fundamental errors in budget setting. If driven by poor property condition, this signals a maintenance backlog. The council is still investigating root causes.
findings.figures: £1,949,000 forecast overspend (PPP £523k, non-PPP £965k, voids £508k)
findings.quote: This has led to insufficient budget allocations in several areas and resulted in a range of under and overspends across the different work streams. The primary areas of overspend forecast due to these factors is the repairs to buildings price per property (PPP) contract being £523,000 overspent and the repairs to buildings non price per property being £965,000 overspent. Void costs have increased and are currently under review to understand the reasons behind this rise. Initial analysis suggests that a significant proportion of these costs may be linked to the condition of properties when they are returned, including instances of tenant damage.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Housing Asset Management Strategy 2025 to 2028
findings.headline: Council acknowledges uncertainty about whether it can meet decarbonisation targets on all properties
findings.detail: The strategy identifies that while some properties can meet mandatory EPC C standard 'with the required investment,' a proportion 'largely due to their construction, regardless of investment will never meet the required standards or become carbon neutral.' The council signals it will need to 'consider alternative long-term strategies' for these properties, implying potential alienations or write-offs.
findings.matters: This signals the HRA portfolio may contain assets that cannot meet statutory energy requirements and may require disposal or costly specialist interventions, affecting long-term asset quality and revenue assumptions.
findings.figures: Target: 100% EPC C or better by March 2029
findings.quote: There is the potential that a proportion of our homes can meet the EPC C government target, with the required investment. There will be properties which, largely due to their construction, regardless of investment will never meet the required standards or become carbon neutral. Therefore, we will need to consider alternative long-term strategies with these properties.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Housing Asset Management Strategy 2025 to 2028
findings.headline: Stock condition data from 2017/18 with only 30% internal inspection coverage, creating forecasting uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's last stock condition survey (2017/18) captured only 30% internal condition data and 100% external data. The strategy acknowledges 'The validity of this data is concerning.' Additionally, approximately 30% of the stock lacks valid EPC data. This poor asset data undermines the reliability of the 30-year investment plan being developed.
findings.matters: A lender assessing HRA viability needs confidence in asset condition forecasts; data this old and incomplete makes medium-term capital planning unreliable. Remedial works could be significantly under or over-estimated.
findings.figures: Last stock condition survey: 2017/18; internal condition data coverage: 30%; external coverage: 100%; properties without EPC on national database: approximately 30% of stock
findings.quote: The data associated with our stock condition is not satisfactory to be used as a robust investment planning tool. A stock survey was last undertaken in 2017/18, and the scope of data collection was constrained. It is understood the levels of information collected for properties internally was 30% and for external aspects 100%. The validity of this data is concerning.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Housing Asset Management Strategy 2025 to 2028
findings.headline: Council acknowledges energy and compliance investment will require additional funding beyond current budget
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly identifies that meeting energy decarbonisation targets and historic component replacement 'will require additional investment and resourcing,' and identifies the need to build 'financial capacity building through more efficient delivery.' This signals a funding gap between current budget and mandatory requirements.
findings.matters: Mandatory EPC C rating by 2030 and compliance obligations are not optional; a council acknowledging it needs additional funding to meet these suggests either current HRA budget constraints or unplanned cost escalation.
findings.figures: PAS2035 retrofit target: 818 retrofits (>15% of stock) by December 2028; EPC C rating target: 100% compliance by March 2029
findings.quote: To meet the energy decarbonisation targets and to address any historic component replacement will require additional investment and resourcing. This will require financial capacity building through more efficient delivery, better data understanding and improved organisation for planned investment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Housing Asset Management Strategy 2025 to 2028
findings.headline: HRA Business Plan reference is six years out of date for a 2025-2028 strategy
findings.detail: The strategy states it has used 'the latest HRA Business Plan (2019)' as reference. This 2019 plan pre-dates the strategy period by six years, suggesting the council's financial planning baseline for housing services may not reflect current circumstances or revenue/capital realities.
findings.matters: The HRA Business Plan is the primary financial and strategic document for housing services; using a 2019 baseline to plan 2025-2028 investments suggests potential disconnects between aspirations and current financial capacity.
findings.figures: HRA Business Plan dated 2019; strategy covers 2025-2028
findings.quote: For the purposes of this strategy, the latest HRA Business Plan (2019) has been used as reference.

findings.headline: New MRP regulations effective 2025-26 restrict how capital receipts can fund revenue minimum revenue provision
findings.detail: Amended MRP legislation published 10 April 2024 introduces restrictions effective from the 2025-26 financial year: capital receipts can no longer be used to directly replace prudent charges to revenue for minimum revenue provision (with only specific legacy exceptions). This changes how councils can manage capital financing and requires Canterbury to reassess its capital strategy.
findings.matters: Regulatory restrictions on capital receipt flexibility reduce the council's financial management options and may increase pressure on revenue budgets to fund capital provision charges going forward
findings.figures: Effective 2025-26 financial year onwards
findings.quote: Capital receipts cannot be used to directly replace, in whole or part, the prudent charge to revenue for MRP (there are specific exceptions for capital loans and leased assets).

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs increased sharply to 5.1%, with peak rates reaching 6% in early 2025
findings.detail: Canterbury's short-term borrowing rose from £27m nine months prior to £31m at year-end, while average rates climbed from 4.7% to 5.1%. Market rates for local authority short-term borrowing spiked notably in late 2024 and early 2025, peaking at around 6% in February and March 2025. This increases the council's revenue costs if forced to refinance or expand short-term debt at prevailing market rates.
findings.matters: Rising short-term borrowing costs directly increase revenue expenditure and reduce financial resilience if the council needs to refinance maturing short-term debt
findings.figures: £31m short-term borrowing at 5.1% (31 March 2025) vs £27m at 4.7% nine months prior; peak rates 6% Feb-Mar 2025
findings.quote: The average rate on the Authority's short-term loans at 31st March 2025 of £31m was 5.1%, this compares with 4.7% on £27m loans 9 months ago.

findings.headline: Whitefriars £75.6m investment producing income below pre-pandemic levels as retail sector pressures persist
findings.detail: The Authority holds a substantial £75.6m investment in the Whitefriars Development Unit Trust, which represents over 40% of the council's total borrowing. The investment generated £5.3m income by March 2025, but income remains below pre-pandemic levels due to ongoing retail sector challenges. The council notes that nationally high street retail rents have been declining, and although Canterbury outperforms national averages, structural headwinds from changing consumer habits and online competition persist. The council is actively revising business plans with its asset management team to explore ways to optimise the use of retail space and ensure long-term sustainability.
findings.matters: A single investment representing over 40% of the council's outstanding debt is experiencing structural income decline, which affects debt service capacity and investment returns.
findings.figures: £75.6m investment; £5.3m income; income below pre-pandemic levels; 41% of £183m total borrowing
findings.quote: While income has steadily improved since the pandemic, it remains below pre-pandemic levels due to ongoing pressures in the retail sector. Nationally, high street retail rents have been declining, driven by changing consumer habits, increased online competition, and economic uncertainty.

findings.headline: External borrowing significantly below forecast, with £15m reduction in Q1
findings.detail: Total external borrowing fell from £183.18m (31 March 2025) to £168.18m (30 June 2025), a £15m Q1 reduction. The council forecast external borrowing would reach £172m by 31 March 2026, but actual borrowing is already below forecast. Short-term borrowing from local authorities fell from £31m to £18m. The council states it 'has not needed to borrow the sums expected in the current financial year,' but does not explain whether this reflects capital programme slippage, improved cash position, or deliberate debt reduction.
findings.matters: Material variance from treasury forecasts indicates either reduced capital programme execution or better-than-expected cash generation. For lenders, understanding the cause is material to assessing the council's capital investment capacity and service delivery timelines.
findings.figures: External borrowing £183.18m (31 March 2025); £168.18m actual (30 June 2025); £172m forecast (31 March 2026)
findings.quote: The council has not needed to borrow the sums expected in the current financial year

findings.headline: CIPFA Code compliance requirement blocks further borrowing until council exits £1.8m commercial property investment
findings.detail: The council holds a £1.84m commercial property generating £250,000 annual net income (13.6% return). CIPFA's 2021 Prudential Code prohibits borrowing to invest primarily for financial return. The council explicitly states it must review exit options before undertaking further borrowing, creating a contingency that could constrain the council's ability to fund capital programmes.
findings.matters: This represents a constraint on borrowing capacity for capital investment until the asset is disposed. For lenders, it signals the council's financial flexibility is restricted by regulatory requirements and may affect capital programme funding.
findings.figures: £1.84 million investment value; £250,000 annual net income; 13.6% rate of return
findings.quote: Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments

findings.headline: Whitefriars strategic investment income remains below pre-pandemic levels due to retail sector pressures
findings.detail: The council's £75.6m investment in Whitefriars Development Unit Trust generated £5.3m income by March 2025 and £2m more by June 2025, but income recovery has stalled. The document notes that income 'remains below pre-pandemic levels due to ongoing pressures in the retail sector,' driven by declining high street rents, online shopping competition, and economic uncertainty. The council is actively revising business plans and optimizing retail space, but these efforts have not yet restored pre-pandemic returns.
findings.matters: This is the council's largest single investment, and returns below expected levels signal structural revenue pressure. For lenders, stable income from core assets is fundamental to creditworthiness and debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £75.6 million investment; £5.3 million income by 31 March 2025; £2m additional by 30 June 2025
findings.quote: While income has steadily improved since the pandemic, it remains below pre-pandemic levels due to ongoing pressures in the retail sector. Nationally, high street retail rents have been declining, driven by changing consumer habits, increased online competition, and economic uncertainty.

news_drafts.headline: Council has committed £20m to Levelling Up Fund capital projects currently in progress.
news_drafts.lead: Large capital commitments carry delivery and financial risk. A lender assesses capital strategy, project delivery track record, and funding sources.

news_drafts.headline: Cyber incident is identified as one of the three highest-scoring risks on the Strategic Risk Register.
news_drafts.lead: Cyber incidents can result in direct financial loss, service disruption, or compliance breaches. Identification as highest risk suggests material vulnerability exposure.

news_drafts.headline: Housing function underwent external governance review by the Housing Regulatory Inspector with formal action plan oversight.
news_drafts.lead: Housing is typically a material financial function for councils. External governance review signals control weaknesses or service problems that could affect financial outcomes or compliance.
